title: Research with Marius
summary: This hub brings together the original MTE/Scudo research and the newer unsafe Rust, FFI, and Crustify work with Marius Momeu. The older documents remain intact: their claims and task statuses are historical notes, not automatically current results.
body:
# Current direction

This hub brings together the original MTE/Scudo research and the newer unsafe Rust, FFI, and Crustify work with Marius Momeu. The older documents remain intact: their claims and task statuses are historical notes, not automatically current results.

## Start here

- [Meeting notes: the two research avenues](#entry=crustify-meeting-avenues): the original notes supplied on November 12, followed by technical clarifications.
- [Crustify research brief](#entry=crustify-research-brief): the new paper, concrete verification obligations, and possible first target.
- [Verification tools and reading map](#entry=crustify-reading-map): which systems help, where their guarantees stop, and sources.
- [First proof experiment and meeting questions](#entry=crustify-first-experiment): a proposed first-week plan, not completed experimental work.

## Two research tracks

**Memory hardening and empirical evaluation:** MTE, Scudo, PAC/BTI, native target studies, reproducible experiments, and testing LLM-generated claims. Use the existing topic filters and original PDFs.

**Unsafe Rust and FFI verification:** model particular failure modes, understand existing verified primitives, then investigate LLM-assisted construction of proofs checked independently. The November 4 discussion narrowed toward this proof-oriented direction, while static analysis remains an alternative avenue.

## Decisions for the next meeting

Choose one actual ffibox primitive and version, one precise safety claim, the C-effect contract, and the proof framework. Decide whether the first claim concerns bounds/initialization/ownership or operational aliasing; those are not interchangeable.

## Evidence labels

Meeting notes record what was discussed. Literature notes report sources and their limits. Proposed experiments are plans until accompanied by checked artifacts and reproducible results. A failure to prove is unknown, not proof of a bug.

## Keeping the hub useful

Use New note for meeting outcomes and Import files for papers or existing Markdown. Tag notes by track and add only genuinely useful entries to the Meeting shortlist. Browser notes are local to this exact site origin; export backups regularly. The existing URL, storage identities, and original files are retained.

title: Meeting notes on the two research avenues
summary: Supplied by Shaurya on November 12, 2026; described as notes from the “last last meeting.” The actual meeting date is unconfirmed. Original wording is preserved below, including shorthand and technical terminology that needs clarification.
body:
# Original meeting notes

Supplied by Shaurya on November 12, 2026; described as notes from the “last last meeting.” The actual meeting date is unconfirmed. Original wording is preserved below, including shorthand and technical terminology that needs clarification.

> Safe rust promises a lot of things: no null-pointer references, no dangling pointers. Easy to constrain the LLMs from reward hacking by asking them to "always build reproducer with Rust annotator, forbid unsafe code"
>
> LLM instructions' find me a reproducer (a comibnation of rust statements) that you can compile with forbid unsafe code), and that triggers a santizier. Not much there; it's a UB.
>
> LLM harness is only a lower bound; doesn't give you complete guarantees. Jusbt becauseyou ask an LLM to look at asnippet of rust code and find issues, it doesn't mean that it doesnt have issues. He wants to look into achieving stronger guarantees by using traditional verification methods (Static analysis, formal verification) along WITH LLMs. This research aims to improve crustify to improve Rust code.
>
> There are two avenues:
> - static analysis (try to extend what the rust compiler already does in Safe Rust, writing our own static analyser that extends those assumptions/properties that the Rust compiler carries on pointers; types, etc, and extend them into C); if the static analysis pass find an execution path that encounters a lifetime that outlives the bound object, that's a candidate for bugs. It's overapproximated (not precise; false positives and/or negatives). Some algorithms are complete and not sound (no false negatives but false positives). To mitigate that, we write tests + ask the LLM to triage these false positives.
> - Formal Verficiation is crazy. We'd need to migrate Rust code AND C code to a formal verification engine (Lean, for example), and express tehse properties as a mathematical expression in Lean's Terms. Then, ask LLM to drive these interactive proofs to prove that this Rust code can NEVER have UB bugs.

# Technical clarifications

## A safe client can expose an unsafe library

A client crate using `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` cannot itself use unsafe code, but it can call safe APIs whose dependencies contain unsafe implementations. Such a client can expose an unsound library or FFI wrapper. This is not evidence that the safe Rust language routinely permits UB: the relevant defect may be in unsafe dependencies, the compiler, or the standard library. A reproducible sanitizer finding is evidence of the specific detected failure, not a universal detector for every kind of UB. Forbidding unsafe client code constrains one form of reward hacking; it does not establish that the target, test oracle, or sanitizer configuration is correct.

## Soundness and completeness need a stated framing

For an overapproximating may-bug analysis, the ideal is to include every modeled execution, possibly reporting paths that cannot occur. This is commonly described as sound analysis with possible false alarms; terminology can reverse depending on whether one is discussing bug reports, a proof procedure, or a classifier. Rather than relying on the labels alone, write the intended guarantee explicitly: which modeled errors can be missed, which false alarms can occur, and under what assumptions? Actual tools may sacrifice coverage or precision. LLM triage is heuristic unless its dismissal is independently justified; it must not silently remove findings from a claimed sound result.

## Proofs establish specified properties under assumptions

Formal verification need not begin by migrating an entire Rust/C program. A modular first step can verify a Rust wrapper under explicit C contracts. The conclusion is conditional on those contracts, the chosen semantics, translation, and trusted checker. “Never has any UB” is much broader than proving one method preserves a buffer invariant.

Sources: [Rust undefined behavior](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html), [Rust unsafe code](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch20-01-unsafe-rust.html), [Static Program Analysis](https://cs.au.dk/~amoeller/spa/).

# Later narrowing

In the [November 4 discussion](https://chatgpt.com/c/6aeaf053-ace8-83e8-9a49-ca7ad63f9a9e?messageId=6cc1c8ad-98b9-421d-b123-a112c2d09374), the immediate assignment narrowed to modeling particular custom-buffer and FFI hazards, studying verified primitives, and proposing proof-oriented approaches before paid LLM experiments. The two avenues above remain the broader context, not two completed implementations.

summary: Start with one actual ffibox buffer primitive and a precisely scoped property. body:
# The concrete opportunity

Start with one actual ffibox buffer primitive and a precisely scoped property. The candidate research question is whether fixed, reviewed C-effect contracts and reusable buffer invariants make LLM-assisted proof construction effective for real Crustify obligations. This is a proposed direction, not an established novelty claim or completed proof.

# Crustify architecture and gaps

The [November 7 Crustify preprint](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10394v1), coauthored by Marius Momeu, describes ffibox ownership/borrowing primitives, Wavefront translation ordering and ownership records, and ffimap unsafe-surface measurement. ffimap is explicitly a linter, not a sound and complete verifier. Section 3.2 identifies missed implicit references from autoref through raw pointers and some unmapped `-sys` structures. Section 5 identifies unsupported owning-element vectors and C-grown arrays through borrowed pointer/count pairs.

Those gaps suggest both possible engineering improvements and a separate checked-contract/proof track. Passing tests and agreeing with generated ownership records do not prove absence of UB.

# A truthful buffer representation

A pointer, length, and capacity are only a starting representation. A useful invariant must establish:

- the allocation identity, extent, alignment, and required access permissions;
- `len <= cap` and a truthful connection between metadata and storage;
- valid initialized elements in the first `len` slots, distinct from spare capacity;
- allocation lifetime, allocator pairing, and exactly-once release where ownership requires it;
- validity of outstanding Rust references and slices during foreign accesses;
- invalidation or replacement of old pointers after storage is freed or reallocated.

For example, a recorded length of 100 does not justify index 75 if only 50 elements are initialized. An index check is useful only after constructors and updates establish the underlying invariant.

[`slice::from_raw_parts`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/slice/fn.from_raw_parts.html) requires valid initialized elements in a single allocation, alignment and a non-null pointer even for an empty slice, an allowed byte extent, and appropriate borrowing conditions. Invalid slice construction can itself violate the contract before indexing.

# Make foreign effects explicit

For each C call, specify which ranges it can read/write, whether it can retain the pointer, free or reallocate storage, invoke callbacks, and what is initialized on return. A proof of Rust under that contract does not automatically establish that the C implementation satisfies it.

A C-side logical-length change is not intrinsically UB. Reallocation, stale metadata, retained pointers, and writes during a conflicting borrow are different hazards. Pin the exact claim and memory model before combining them.

# Keep two proof tracks distinct

**Buffer invariant track:** establish initialization, truthful bounds, allocation ownership, and operation-specific invariants.

**Operational aliasing track:** establish that concrete accesses obey a pinned pointer-permission model such as Tree Borrows. A proof of bounds or ownership does not silently settle every operational aliasing rule. Rust's exact aliasing rules remain incompletely specified in the [Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html).

# Research status

This brief is a literature synthesis prepared November 12, 2026. No new proof experiments or paid API calls were run for it. The first primitive, framework, aliasing model, C assumptions, and evaluation suite remain choices for Marius and Shaurya.

title: Verification tools and reading map
summary: [RustBelt, POPL 2018](https://plv.mpi-sws.org/rustbelt/popl18/paper.pdf) models ownership and sharing as logical resources and proves selected modeled unsafe libraries uphold safe-client guarantees. It is not a proof of all current Rust, its compiler, and its standard library. Read it for the distinction between knowing an address and having permission to access a resource.
body:
# Start with existing verified primitives

[RustBelt, POPL 2018](https://plv.mpi-sws.org/rustbelt/popl18/paper.pdf) models ownership and sharing as logical resources and proves selected modeled unsafe libraries uphold safe-client guarantees. It is not a proof of all current Rust, its compiler, and its standard library. Read it for the distinction between knowing an address and having permission to access a resource.

[RefinedRust, PLDI 2024](https://plv.mpi-sws.org/refinedrust/paper-refinedrust.pdf) is a particularly close buffer template. Its simplified vector separates allocation and deallocation resources from initialized contents, spare storage, length, and borrowing obligations. Read Section 3 and Figure 4. It is not a proof of all upstream `Vec`, and it leaves a full operational aliasing model outside its account.

The [October 2026 RefinedRust extension](https://iris-project.org/pdfs/2026-oopsla-refinedrust2.pdf) adds traits, closures, and iterators and evaluates memory-management code. Frontend encoding and underlying semantics still belong to the trust story; slice/unsized support needs attention for the chosen target.

# Framework choices

- **RefinedRust/Rocq:** strongest existing match for a real unsafe buffer proof about metadata, initialization, or ownership. Reproduce an existing proof before adding an LLM.
- **Small Lean model:** useful for learning and testing invariants, but proving the model is not yet proving ffibox source. Avoid building a whole translator as the first project.
- **[AutoCorrode/Isabelle](https://github.com/awslabs/AutoCorrode):** credible separation-logic infrastructure with a µRust frontend, not arbitrary Rust/C import. Existing group expertise should influence the choice.
- **[Aeneas](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas):** valuable safe-Rust work; do not assume arbitrary unsafe ffibox internals are already supported.
- **[lean-miri](https://github.com/proofs-rs/lean-miri):** new MIR-to-Lean experimental direction introduced November 5. Its status distinguishes importing, executing, and proving. Successful process exit can coexist with incomplete guest execution; treat this as a feasibility lead, not a mature universal verifier.

# Aliasing and mixed-language baselines

[Tree Borrows, PLDI 2025](https://plf.inf.ethz.ch/research/pldi25-tree-borrows.html) supplies a model and Rocq artifact. [Towards verifying unsafe Rust programs against Rust’s pointer-aliasing restrictions](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.28326v1) is work in progress; implementation and soundness goals must not be treated as completed support.

[MiriLLI](https://github.com/icmccorm/mirilli) combines Rust and LLVM interpretation for dynamic mixed-language checking. Its [study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11671) gives realistic failure examples, not universal proof. [Miri native-library support](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri) is explicitly experimental with tracking limitations; a clean native FFI run is not an aliasing certificate.

[Crema](https://github.com/AFx3/crema-static-analyzer) targets cross-language heap management including leaks, double-free, and UAF; it is early-stage and not a full aliasing verifier. [FFIChecker](https://github.com/lizhuohua/rust-ffi-checker) is an older LLVM-based baseline with pinned-toolchain compatibility costs. [BorrowSanitizer](https://goals.rust-lang.org/2026/borrowsanitizer.html) is important ongoing dynamic aliasing work; planned feature parity is not established completion. [Kani foreign stubs](https://model-checking.github.io/kani/reference/experimental/stubbing.html) enable reduced checks, but prove against the replacement model unless a separate argument connects it to C.

# Closest LLM work and the novelty question

[Aria](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.06341v1) reports kernel-checked reconstruction of RustBelt/Iris lemmas with an agent harness. [KaPilot](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.21957v1) studies unsafe-Rust specification generation and Kani checking. [A Rust-to-Lean AI-prover experience report](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.30106v1) combines extraction, specifications, generated proofs, and kernel checking, but does not currently cover unsafe Rust.

Therefore “an LLM writes proofs” is not enough as a contribution. Focus on real Crustify contracts, reusable invariants, checked assumptions, and an evaluation that distinguishes proof success from vacuous specifications.

# Suggested reading order

1. Crustify §§3.2, 4.6, 5 and Appendix E: architecture and its actual limits.
2. Rust slice safety contract and undefined-behavior reference: enumerate obligations.
3. RefinedRust §3/Fig. 4: buffer representation; then its limitations and 2026 extension.
4. RustBelt: ownership/sharing and abstraction soundness.
5. Aria and KaPilot: what existing LLM proof/specification work already does.
6. Tree Borrows and MiriLLI if the chosen first target is operational aliasing.

title: First proof experiment and meeting questions
summary: This is a proposed plan, not an experiment already executed.
body:
# Proposed first week

This is a proposed plan, not an experiment already executed.

1. **Choose and freeze one target.** Pick an actual ffibox method and commit. Specify whether the first claim is bounds/initialization/ownership or operational aliasing. Record permitted C effects and excluded behaviors.
2. **Reproduce a small existing checked example.** Verify the environment before asking an LLM to construct anything. Prefer a tiny buffer example in the framework the team knows.
3. **Write one reviewed specification manually.** Record an assumption ledger covering C, allocator, translation, memory model, toolchain, and trusted checker. Include examples satisfying the preconditions to expose vacuity.
4. **Build correct and broken pairs.** Candidate mutations include stale length after resize, treating capacity as initialized length, losing an allocation on failed reallocation, retaining an invalidated pointer, or duplicate ownership. Choose only cases actually represented by the model.
5. **Add a proof-only LLM harness.** The model may edit approved proof files, not the code, theorem, assumptions, or foreign contract. Reject `admit`/`sorry`, added axioms, unapproved imports, and specification weakening. Check from a clean immutable target, inspect theorem dependencies, and retain the proof artifacts.
6. **Compare fixed-budget baselines.** No-LLM automation, one-shot LLM, and verifier-feedback LLM. Record checked proof rate, time, tokens/cost, human annotation effort, unsupported cases, invalid-change attempts, and counterexamples separately.

# Interpret the outcomes honestly

A checked proof establishes the stated property under its assumptions. A bounded check is bounded. A dynamic failure is an observed counterexample under its detector/model. A timeout or unsuccessful proof attempt is unknown, not evidence that the implementation is buggy. A system accepting both correct and broken versions has not succeeded merely because its output sounds convincing.

For an aliasing-only pilot, initially exclude concurrency, pointer-integer casts, reallocation, and UnsafeCell; pin a Tree Borrows version and model explicit create/pass/access/return permission transitions. Extend only after the narrow semantics are working.

# Questions for Marius

- Which concrete ffibox primitive and branch should be first?
- Is the initial deliverable a buffer-invariant proof or an operational aliasing result?
- Which C contracts can be assumed, and which C behavior needs verification?
- Does the group have reusable Rocq/Lean/Isabelle artifacts or a preferred framework?
- What would count as a useful contribution beyond Aria and KaPilot?
- Should ffimap implicit-reference blind spots be a secondary engineering task?
- Can the first milestone be one small checked theorem plus a seeded-bug suite, before paid model experiments?

# Short meeting summary

“I looked at how verified Rust buffers separate allocation ownership from initialized contents. A bounds check alone is not enough unless the metadata and access permissions are truthful. I would start with one Crustify primitive and an explicit C-effect contract, freeze the specification, then let the LLM construct a proof checked independently. RefinedRust is the closest buffer model I found, but its aliasing scope matters, so I’d like to choose the first safety claim carefully.”

# Read this first

A beginner-friendly guide to the research, from memory safety and Rust ownership through unsafe code, FFI, static analysis, formal verification, and the proposed Crustify experiment. No prior Rust or proof-assistant knowledge is assumed.

## Reading paths

- **Learn from scratch:** Chapters 1–5 explain the foundations.
- **Understand the research:** Chapters 6–8 connect those foundations to the project and tools.
- **Prepare for the call:** Chapter 11 gives the short summary and meeting agenda.
- **Plan the work:** Chapters 9–10 describe the proposed experiment and evaluation.
- **Look up a term or source:** use the glossary and linked reading list at the end.

Open the original PDF above for the fully formatted 15-page guide. All pages are also searchable below. The tool choices and experimental plan are proposals, not claims of completed proofs or experiments.
pages:
MARIUS RESEARCH • LEARNING GUIDE



Understanding Rust and Crustify Research
A beginner guide to your work with Marius
Prepared for Shaurya Verma • November 12 2026
This document explains the ideas behind your Marius research from the beginning. You do not need prior Rust
or formal verification experience. It connects the language basics to your meeting notes, the new Crustify
research, and a small experiment you could propose on your call.

The recommendation in one paragraph
Start with one real Crustify buffer operation, write down exactly what must remain true about its memory and
what C is allowed to do, and try to establish that property with an independent verification tool. Only then add
an LLM to help construct the proof. This keeps the problem small enough to learn from and makes the result
more meaningful than asking a model whether code looks safe.

What is established and what is proposed
   Your meeting notes and November 4 chat establish the motivation: combine LLMs with traditional
    verification, with a later emphasis on modeling hazards and exploring checked proofs.
   The literature survey identifies relevant models, tools, and their stated limits. Numbered references at the
    end link to primary sources and your earlier discussion.
   The experiment, tool recommendation, and first week plan are proposals. No new verifier installation,
    Crustify code experiment, completed proof, or paid API experiment is reported here.

How to use this guide
Read Chapters 1–5 for the foundations. Chapters 6–8 explain what the research is actually trying to do.
Chapters 9–11 give the concrete experiment, evaluation, and meeting agenda. The final pages contain a
glossary and a reading list.
If the call is imminent, read Chapter 11 first. Its summary is deliberately modest about what has been
accomplished and specific about what to ask Marius.




                                                                     Shaurya Verma • November 12 2026 • 1

MARIUS RESEARCH • LEARNING GUIDE


1 Why memory safety is a research problem
A program stores data in memory. A pointer identifies where some data lives. An allocation is a region of
storage reserved for a value or collection of values. The difficult part is not merely finding an address; it is
knowing whether the storage still exists, whether it contains a valid value, and whether this part of the
program is allowed to access it now.

Four failures to recognize
   Out of bounds: reading element 12 of a buffer that only contains 10 elements. A numeric address might
    exist, but it is outside the storage the operation is allowed to use.
   Use after free: using a pointer after its allocation has been released. The address might now hold unrelated
    data, or appear to work until the allocator reuses it.
   Double free: releasing the same allocation twice. Two pieces of code may each mistakenly believe they
    own it.
   Invalid aliasing: using multiple access paths in a way that violates the language’s rules. In Rust, these rules
    can matter even if every address is inside a live allocation.

Undefined behavior is not just a crash
Undefined behavior, usually shortened to UB, means an execution violates requirements on which the
language and its compiler rely. The language no longer promises the ordinary behavior you expect. A crash is
one possible result, but silent wrong output or surprising optimization effects are possible too. “It ran correctly
on my machine” is therefore weak evidence about the absence of UB. [2]
A normal handled error is different. For example, safe Rust indexing can panic when an index is out of range. A
panic is a specified failure mechanism, not automatically undefined behavior. Similarly, leaking memory is
undesirable but does not by itself violate Rust’s memory-safety guarantee.

How this relates to your earlier MTE and Scudo work
MTE is hardware memory tagging, and Scudo is a hardened allocator. Those kinds of defenses can detect or
mitigate classes of memory misuse at runtime. This new direction asks a different question: can we establish,
before or beyond a particular run, that a small program component obeys a precise safety property?
Detection, mitigation, and proof can complement each other. None should be described as interchangeable.

The central question
Can we replace “we tried some inputs and found no problem” with a defensible statement about every
execution covered by an explicit model and its assumptions? That last phrase matters: even a formal proof is
only as broad as the theorem, model, and trusted assumptions behind it.




                                                                         Shaurya Verma • November 12 2026 • 2

MARIUS RESEARCH • LEARNING GUIDE


2 The Rust basics you need first
Rust aims to make memory-safe programming practical without requiring a garbage collector. Its compiler
tracks ownership and borrowing. You can think of ownership as responsibility for a value, including when its
resources should be released. Borrowing is temporary access without taking over that responsibility. [1]

Ownership and moving a value
let a = String::from("hello");
let b = a;          // Ownership moves to b.
// println!("{a}"); // Rejected: a no longer owns the String.
println!("{b}");

A String owns heap storage. Moving it does not mean two independent owners may later free the same buffer.
The old binding can no longer be used as its owner. Some simple types, such as integers, implement Copy, so
assignment copies them instead. Do not generalize the String example to every type.

Shared and mutable borrowing
let mut values = vec![10, 20, 30];
let first = &values[0]; // Shared reference to an element.
println!("{first}");
values.push(40);        // Fine after that borrow is no longer used.

The ampersand creates a reference. An &T reference provides shared access; an &mut T reference provides
exclusive access for mutation. Rust normally allows either shared references or an exclusive mutable reference
to the same relevant data while those borrows are active. There are carefully controlled interior-mutability
mechanisms, but they are not the starting point for our first experiment.
Why care about push? Growing a vector may require moving its elements to a new allocation. A reference into
the old allocation must not remain usable after that happens. Rust’s borrow checker rejects ordinary safe-code
patterns that would create this conflict.

Lifetimes describe validity relationships
A lifetime is not simply a timer or a variable’s lexical scope. It expresses how long a reference can validly be
used and how that validity relates to other values. A function must not return a reference to a local allocation
that is destroyed when the function returns. The compiler can infer many lifetime relationships; explicit
lifetime annotations describe relationships rather than extending an allocation’s life.

Three types you will keep seeing
   Vec<T> is a growable sequence of T values. Its length is the number of initialized elements; its capacity is
    the space it has reserved.
   A slice, written &[T] or &mut [T], is a borrowed view of consecutive elements. It does not automatically
    own the allocation.
   A raw pointer, written *const T or *mut T, does not carry the same compiler-enforced borrowing
    guarantees as a reference. It can exist without being safe to dereference.




                                                                      Shaurya Verma • November 12 2026 • 3

MARIUS RESEARCH • LEARNING GUIDE


3 Safe Rust and unsafe implementations
Safe Rust code cannot directly perform certain operations that require the programmer to uphold extra
obligations, such as dereferencing an arbitrary raw pointer. Unsafe Rust permits those operations in explicit
unsafe contexts. It does not turn off the language’s rules or make undefined behavior acceptable. [1, 2]

A safe interface may contain unsafe code inside
A standard collection can provide a safe method while its implementation uses raw pointers internally. The
library author is responsible for making every allowed use of that safe method uphold the required invariants.
“Sound abstraction” means that safe callers cannot use the interface, within its stated safe contract, to trigger
undefined behavior through an invalid implementation.
That is why your meeting note about a safe reproducer is useful. A small client containing only safe Rust can
still expose a bug in a library’s unsafe internals. The defect would be in the unsafe abstraction or another
trusted component, not evidence that arbitrary correct safe Rust routinely permits memory corruption.

What forbid unsafe code does and does not show
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]

fn main() {
    // Call safe APIs here.
    // The dependency may contain unsafe internals.
}

The attribute forbids unsafe code in the scope to which it applies. Putting it in the reproducer crate helps stop
a model from “winning” by inserting an obviously unsafe raw-pointer operation into its own test. It does not
recursively prove that every dependency is safe, and it does not make a sanitizer omniscient.
A useful reproducer must satisfy several independent checks: the intended restrictions really apply, the client
uses the allowed API, the relevant sanitizer or interpreter runs, and the reported failure is relevant to the
property being investigated. Compiler success alone is not that evidence.

The LLM harness is a search procedure
Your note proposes asking the LLM to find a compilable combination of Rust statements that triggers a
checker. That is a bug-finding strategy. A successful, validated counterexample can be valuable. An
unsuccessful search only says that this search did not find a counterexample with its time, tools, and inputs. It
does not prove that no counterexample exists.
This is the meaning of the “lower bound” intuition: confirmed failures show at least those failures exist; the
number found does not measure every latent bug. A stronger method must reason about executions the
model never explicitly wrote or ran.

A practical warning about reward hacking
The model could weaken the test, change the target, suppress the checker, or use an irrelevant crash.
Restricting unsafe code is one guardrail, not a complete defense. Keep the target and acceptance checks
outside the model’s writable scope and validate its outputs independently.



                                                                      Shaurya Verma • November 12 2026 • 4

MARIUS RESEARCH • LEARNING GUIDE


4 The Rust and C boundary
FFI means foreign function interface: the mechanism that lets code in one language call code in another.
Crustify’s setting involves Rust and C. A Rust wrapper may call C to allocate, fill, resize, or free a buffer. The
Rust compiler cannot infer all the facts about an arbitrary C implementation that it normally tracks for ordinary
safe Rust.

The wrapper needs more than a function signature
Suppose C receives a pointer and a length. Will it only read those bytes? Can it modify them? Will it save the
pointer for later? Can it free or reallocate the buffer? Can it call back into Rust while the operation is in
progress? These behaviors can change whether a Rust reference is valid. The argument types alone often do
not express enough.
An effect contract records those answers. It describes the permitted effects and the state guaranteed on
return. A Rust-side proof can assume that contract, but a separate argument is needed to show that the real C
implementation obeys it. Otherwise the result is explicitly conditional.

A reallocation example
Before C call: ptr A --> allocation A
Rust view:    &data --> allocation A

C may resize:      ptr B --> allocation B
                   allocation A may be freed

Danger:            old Rust view still refers to A

The bug is not that C changed a number. The bug is using a view whose storage or access permissions are no
longer valid. Reallocation can sometimes keep the same numeric address, but a sound argument cannot rely
on that accidental outcome. Allocation identity and provenance matter as well as the address.

Three separate obligations
   Storage: the region must exist, have the right extent and alignment, and stay alive for the access.
   Contents: the accessed elements must be initialized and valid for their type.
   Permissions: the access must respect the applicable borrowing and aliasing rules, including effects of other
    access paths.
A proof of one does not automatically prove the other two. For example, an in-bounds write through C may
still conflict with a live shared Rust reference. Conversely, changing an unrelated C-side metadata field is not
automatically an aliasing violation.

Why this is a good research target
The boundary concentrates assumptions that are easy to overlook in code review. If we can represent those
assumptions precisely for a small reusable buffer abstraction, we may help many translated callers without
having to prove an entire mixed-language application at once.




                                                                       Shaurya Verma • November 12 2026 • 5

MARIUS RESEARCH • LEARNING GUIDE


5 What Crustify does
Crustify is the translation research system discussed with Marius. The November 7 2026 preprint describes
translating C into Rust while managing ownership and the remaining unsafe boundary. Its relevance here is not
that translation eliminates the need for verification. It is that the generated code and reusable primitives
provide concrete targets for it. [4]

The three components relevant to your project
   ffibox provides ownership and borrowing primitives intended to avoid creating Rust references into
    memory that C may still alias. The exact guarantee depends on the specific primitive and how callers use it.
   Wavefront handles dependency ordering and uses agent-authored ownership information during the
    translation process. An ownership record is useful guidance, but agreement with a generated record is not
    itself proof that the record is correct.
   ffimap measures parts of the unsafe surface. The paper explicitly describes it as a linter rather than a
    sound and complete verifier. A lower count of risky constructs is not a theorem that the remaining
    program has no UB.

Specific gaps reported by the paper
The paper reports that ffimap misses some implicit references formed by autoref through raw pointers and
references involving some unmapped -sys structures. Autoref means Rust inserts a reference implicitly for an
operation, so looking only for an explicit ampersand can miss it. A -sys crate commonly contains low-level
foreign-library bindings.
The paper also identifies unsupported ffibox cases, including owning-element vectors and arrays that C grows
through a borrowed pointer and count. These are useful leads to discuss, not evidence that every existing
ffibox use is broken. We have not reproduced these cases or inspected every artifact repository in this research
pass.

Two different kinds of contribution
An engineering contribution could improve a documented blind spot in ffimap or extend a primitive. A
verification contribution could establish a precisely stated property of an existing primitive and develop a
repeatable checked-proof workflow. Both could help Crustify, but they answer different questions and need
different evaluation.

My recommendation for your call
Ask Marius for one actual method, the current branch, and a realistic allowed C behavior. The best first target
is small enough that a human can understand its contract and that a deliberately broken version can be
constructed. Avoid committing to “prove Crustify safe” before you know the representation, supported
language features, and proof infrastructure.
The narrow initial claim might be: this resize wrapper preserves an initialized-buffer invariant under a stated
allocation contract. That is much more actionable than “Rust code can never have UB,” and it makes the
remaining assumptions visible.

6 Your meeting notes explained and clarified
Your notes describe two avenues: extending static analysis across Rust and C, and using formal verification
with LLM-assisted proofs. Your later November 4 discussion emphasizes first studying verified primitives,
modeling the hazards, and choosing a plan before API-key experiments. These are related directions, not
evidence that both full systems have already been designed. [3]

Avenue one is static analysis
Static analysis examines a program without running each possible execution. An analysis might track which
allocation a pointer refers to, which calls can free it, and whether a later access can use it after its lifetime
ends. To scale, it usually merges many possible runtime states into an abstract representation.
Imagine a branch where only one path frees a pointer. If the analyzer cannot establish which branch will be
taken, it may conservatively retain both possibilities. A later read becomes a warning. If that branch is
impossible for real inputs, the warning is a false positive. This is a common cost of overapproximating possible
behavior.
Your notes use “complete and not sound” for “no false negatives but false positives.” Terminology varies with
what the procedure is deciding, so avoid using that label alone. For a may-bug analysis intended to cover all
modeled executions, the usual sound-overapproximation goal is no missed modeled behavior, accepting
possible false alarms. Concrete tools can still miss bugs because of unsupported features, unsound shortcuts,
or inadequate models.
An LLM could propose tests or explain why a warning seems infeasible. But its opinion is not a proof that a
warning is false. A robust workflow keeps an unresolved category and requires independently checkable
evidence before dismissing a warning.

Avenue two is formal verification
Formal verification states a property mathematically and checks a proof against a model. The hard part
includes expressing the real program and its memory behavior accurately, not just writing the final proof. Lean,
Rocq, and Isabelle are proof-assistant ecosystems, not magic importers that automatically understand
arbitrary Rust and C.
An LLM can propose proof steps, helper lemmas, annotations, or candidate contracts. A trusted checker can
reject an invalid proof step. But it cannot rescue the wrong theorem: if the theorem assumes away the bug or
models the wrong program, a valid proof can still be irrelevant to the real system.

How the two avenues fit together
Static analysis can find candidate obligations or select a suspicious method. Formal verification can establish a
deeper property for a restricted target. Tests and dynamic checkers can expose mistakes in implementations
or models. The research need not discard testing; it should state exactly what each type of evidence
establishes.

7 What a proof would actually look like
A useful specification has preconditions, postconditions, and an invariant. Preconditions are facts required
before an operation. Postconditions describe what it guarantees afterward. An invariant is a fact that must
remain true at the boundaries where the abstraction promises it, often before and after every public
operation.

A small initialized buffer invariant
For a byte buffer, let p identify storage, n be its initialized length, and c be its capacity. A first invariant could
require 0 ≤ n ≤ c; a live allocation large enough for c bytes; valid initialized contents in the prefix [0, n); correct
ownership for destruction; and no outstanding access that conflicts with the operation being performed.
capacity c = 8
index       0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
contents    A B C D ? ? ? ?
length n = 4

[0, n) is readable data
[n, c) is reserved space, not necessarily readable data

If a read receives an index i with 0 ≤ i < n, the invariant tells us the element exists and is initialized. The index
check alone would not establish that. Constructors must create the invariant, mutations must preserve it, and
destruction must consume ownership correctly.

An illustrative theorem rather than a finished proof
“For every state satisfying BufferInvariant, and every index below its length, read returns the corresponding
stored byte without violating the modeled memory rules, provided the foreign code obeys the stated effect
contract.” This sentence makes the quantification and assumptions visible. A real theorem would also name
the program semantics and treatment of failures.
The first model can use bytes to avoid extra complications of arbitrary T values, destructors, and type validity.
Restricting the first target is legitimate if the restriction is explicit. It is not legitimate to later describe the
result as covering every Rust type or arbitrary C callbacks.

Why kernel checking is useful but not enough
A proof assistant’s kernel checks that a proof follows its logical rules. This can make an LLM’s confidence
irrelevant: invalid proof steps fail. However, the total trusted chain still includes the statement, imported
axioms, formal semantics, and whatever translation connects the real source to the model. Those assumptions
must be documented.

Vacuous success is a real failure mode
If the precondition accidentally says n < 0 and n ≥ 0, there are no allowed states. A theorem can then hold
without telling us anything about real buffers. Similarly, assuming “this pointer is always valid” may hide
precisely the property we hoped to establish. Test that ordinary intended states satisfy the preconditions, and
review assumptions separately from proof success.

8 Choosing an initial verification approach
RefinedRust and Rocq are the closest buffer starting point
RustBelt models ownership and sharing logically to justify safe interfaces implemented with unsafe code.
RefinedRust builds a more automated verification approach and includes a simplified Rustonomicon vector
example. Its representation separates allocation ownership from initialized contents and spare capacity. That is
unusually relevant to the buffer question here. [5, 6]
Important limits remain. The example is not a proof of the entire production standard-library vector. The
published scope excludes a complete operational aliasing model and some validity and pointer-cast details. A
successful proof in that model must not be advertised as full Tree Borrows compliance. A 2026 extension
improves practical support, but frontend correspondence and parts of the semantic infrastructure remain
trusted. [7]

Lean is useful for an explicit small model
A hand-written Lean model could represent allocation identities, initialized ranges, and allowed operations
clearly. It may be the quickest way to learn the invariant and exercise a proof-generation loop. But a proof
about that model does not automatically verify the actual ffibox source. Keep the model-to-source
correspondence as a separate obligation.
The new lean-miri project is worth a feasibility look, not an assumption of mature support. Its own status
distinguishes importing MIR, executing code, and proving a safety theorem. A successful process exit is not
enough to establish completed guest execution or universal correctness. [17]

Isabelle and other systems
AutoCorrode is relevant separation-logic infrastructure with a restricted Rust-oriented frontend. It is not an
arbitrary Rust/C verifier. Aeneas is useful related work for safe Rust, but its stated current scope should not be
confused with automatic verification of arbitrary unsafe ffibox internals. Choose infrastructure partly based on
what Marius and the group already know. [8, 9]

Keep operational aliasing as a separate decision
If the main theorem is about aliasing permissions, choose and pin the aliasing model. Tree Borrows provides a
specific model and formalization. A recent separation-logic proposal for unsafe Rust is work in progress rather
than a completed general verifier. Do not call a proof about length arithmetic an aliasing proof. [15, 16]

My recommendation
First explore whether a small real primitive fits the existing RefinedRust buffer approach. If setup or
unsupported features dominate, use a small explicit model to learn the proof obligations, while clearly labeling
the source-correspondence gap. Do not begin by building a whole Rust and C translator. Ask Marius to choose
whether the first milestone prioritizes a real-source theorem or a clear proof-of-concept model.

9 Related tools and the novelty question
Dynamic and static baselines
Miri interprets Rust and can catch many invalid executions. Its experimental native-library support has
important tracking limitations, so passing it is not a certificate for arbitrary native C behavior. MiriLLI combines
Rust and LLVM interpretation for mixed-language executions; it is a useful dynamic baseline, not proof over all
executions. [10, 11]
Crema is an early-stage static analyzer targeting cross-language heap-management issues such as leaks, use
after free, and double free. Its stated scope does not equal complete Rust reference-aliasing verification.
FFIChecker is another related cross-language memory-management analyzer with an older pinned toolchain.
Compatibility work may be necessary before either is usable on current artifacts. [12, 13]
Kani can check a bounded or otherwise explicitly modeled Rust harness and supports foreign-function stubs. A
stub is a replacement model of C behavior. A checked result applies to that replacement unless a separate
argument connects it to real C. Record bounds and assumptions instead of reporting simply “proved safe.” [14]

LLM assisted proof construction already exists
Aria reports agent-assisted reconstruction of RustBelt and Iris proofs checked by a proof system. KaPilot
studies generating specifications for unsafe Rust with Kani. These make “we used an LLM to write Rust proofs”
insufficient as a novelty claim. Their reported results also do not imply that arbitrary new mixed Rust/C
programs are solved. [18, 19]
The promising question is more specific: can reviewed C-effect contracts and reusable buffer invariants help an
LLM construct checked proofs for actual Crustify primitives, while detecting inadequate specifications and
invalid implementation changes? The contribution could be in the modeling, automation, real target coverage,
or evaluation. That novelty still needs confirmation with Marius and a deeper related-work review.

Other leads worth keeping in the hub
BorrowSanitizer targets aliasing detection in mixed-language settings, and SafeFFI studies practical sanitizer
placement at boundaries into safe pointer types. They are important comparisons if the project shifts toward
runtime instrumentation. Neither should be presented as interchangeable with a universal proof of the
proposed wrapper. [20, 21]

The standard for a useful result
It is more convincing to verify one real property, expose the assumptions, and show that meaningful broken
variants fail than to generate many persuasive-looking proofs of weak statements. Tool failure and proof
failure must remain distinct from demonstrated bugs. Unsupported targets are valuable information about
feasibility, not something to silently remove from the denominator.

10 The proposed first experiment
This is a plan, not an experiment already performed. Start with one byte-buffer operation and exclude
concurrency, callbacks, arbitrary pointer-integer casts, and complex element destructors unless the chosen
target requires them. If those features are central, choose a different first target or explicitly budget the

Step one is to freeze the target and claim
Get the exact ffibox method, repository version, and expected C behavior from Marius. Write the intended
property in plain English before choosing proof syntax. Decide whether the operation must preserve bounds,
initialized contents, ownership, or operational aliasing. List the properties intentionally left outside the first
theorem.

Step two is to reproduce an existing checked example
Build a tiny example in the selected framework and rerun its original checks. Record tool versions and
commands. This tests whether the infrastructure works before asking an LLM to solve an unfamiliar target.
Then write or adapt a reviewed specification for the real method.

Step three is to use correct and broken pairs
   Correct resize versus a version that keeps using an old pointer after a successful moving reallocation.
   Correct failure handling versus a version that loses or incorrectly frees the original allocation on resize
    failure. Use the actual allocator contract, not an assumed generic realloc behavior.
   Correct initialized-length update versus a version that claims uninitialized spare capacity is valid readable
    data.
   Correct ownership release versus a version that permits two owners to free the same allocation.
Not every framework can express every mutant. Report that limitation. A failure to verify a broken program is
not automatically a counterexample; the tool may simply be incomplete or time out. Where possible, obtain a
concrete failing execution or a precise violated obligation.

Step four is to add the LLM only to proof construction
Keep the program, theorem, contracts, imports, and acceptance policy fixed. Let the model propose proof
steps or approved helper lemmas. Reject attempts to add unchecked assumptions, use proof escape hatches,
change the target, or relax preconditions. Check the result in a fresh environment so stale build artifacts
cannot masquerade as success.

Step five is to compare fairly
Compare baseline automation, a one-shot model attempt, and a model with verifier feedback under equal
budgets. Measure accepted proofs, human specification effort, time, tokens or cost, unsupported cases, and
invalid-edit attempts. Review which theorem was actually checked and what assumptions it depends on. This is
the beginning of an evaluation, not a promise of publication-ready results in a week.

12 Glossary and self check
Allocation. A reserved region of memory. It has an identity and lifetime, not just an address.
Aliasing. Multiple ways to reach the same memory. Whether particular accesses are allowed depends on
language rules and permissions.
Borrow. Access to a value without taking ownership. Shared and exclusive borrowing have different rules.
Contract. An explicit statement of required inputs or state and permitted effects or guaranteed results.
Counterexample. A concrete execution or model state that violates a claimed property.
Invariant. A property maintained at the relevant boundaries of an abstraction or loop.
Lemma. A helper theorem used to prove another theorem.
MIR and LLVM IR. Intermediate program representations used by compiler and analysis tools. Importing either
does not alone prove correspondence to all source behavior.
Provenance. Information about a pointer’s origin or allocation relationship that can matter beyond its numeric
address.
Reproducer. A small program that reliably demonstrates a particular observed problem.
Sanitizer. Instrumentation or a runtime checker that detects certain invalid behaviors on executions it
observes.
Trusted computing base. The components and assumptions the result relies on rather than independently
proves.
Vacuous proof. A logically valid result that says little about intended behavior, for example because its
assumptions permit no real case.

Check whether the main ideas make sense
Why is index < len insufficient by itself? Because the allocation and initialized-length metadata must be valid,
and access permissions must hold. Why is no sanitizer failure insufficient? Because only particular executions
and checks were exercised. Why can a checked proof still miss the point? Because it may prove the wrong
statement, use unrealistic assumptions, or lack a justified connection to the real source.
What is the first research deliverable? A small, explicit target and property with a reproducible checking
procedure, not a blanket assurance that generated Rust is safe.
